questions.worked_solution:
We need to calculate the product of $-3.2$ with itself:

$$
(-3.2)^{2}=(-3.2)\cdot (-3.2)=(3.2)\cdot (3.2)
$$

First, we ignore the decimal points and multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,9\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,6\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $32\times 32=1\,024.$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in the first factor ($3.2$) and $1$ decimal place in the second factor ($3.2$), so their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

We take our value of $1\,024$ and insert a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places:

$$
10\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{24}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Therefore, ${3.2}^{2}=10.24.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To **square** a number means to multiply that number by itself. 

For example, to "square $3$", we need to multiply $3$ by $3.$ We write the "square of $3$" as $3^2,$ so we have

$$
3^2 = 3 \cdot 3 = {\color{blue}9}.
$$

We would then say that "the square of $3$ is $9$". We could also say "$3$ squared equals $9$".

The number $\color{blue}2$ in the expression $3^{\color{blue}2}$ is called the **power** or **exponent**.

The act of squaring a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $3$ with the following collection of three items:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/4a4dbb46401052829138bddc1653ae843babf4c5cfb6ba9fc40ca29ede99bd70.png)

Then we can picture $3^2$ by creating a square with length and height both equal to $3\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/cc343eafb463e25ab429bafbc06216dad73037e5a02a2be9adfe046629636013.png)

There are $9$ items in total in our square, indicating that $3^2 = 9.$

The first few basic squares are shown below:

| $1^2=1 \cdot 1={\color{blue}1}$ | $2^2=2 \cdot 2={\color{blue}4}$ | $3^2=3 \cdot 3={\color{blue}9}$ | $4^2=4 \cdot 4={\color{blue}16}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/ce5db07809eb56891f31ac7fb0257edb42bd650f00c51c25857b02d1333165ad.png) | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/6113e94a28fc50c7f1fe77ddf082d28d543aa9e2b6e65f82e8623a89f624f7db.png) | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/cc343eafb463e25ab429bafbc06216dad73037e5a02a2be9adfe046629636013.png) | ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14147553/assets/7d56b21746fa8a0053fa32b6c2bc6d9393e13459cb65473e64589cc2f6a01ad3.png) |

The squares of our usual counting numbers are called **square numbers** or **perfect squares**. We can write them as follows:

$$
1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2, 5^2, 6^2, \ldots \qquad \text{or} \qquad {\color{blue}1}, {\color{blue}4}, {\color{blue}9}, {\color{blue}16}, {\color{blue}25}, {\color{blue}36}, \ldots
$$

tutorials.name: Squaring Negative Numbers
tutorials.problem:
The squares of negative numbers are always positive because a negative times a negative is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\end{aligned}
$$

Some squares of negative numbers are as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{3}^{2} & =(-1)\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 9 \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
